utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Krajisnik, I do understand that we received another CD with documents, an index more or less, a short description has been provided. May I take it, Mr. Josse, that you take care that the index at least is translated with full priority so that everyone knows what's on the CD.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are having it summarised at the moment. Would that suffice, Your Honour? To have the full translation will not be easy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, most important is that we know what is on the CD approximately. Could be that it's material that is already in evidence. From what I saw today, there might be well quite some matters which are already in evidence, so that we at least can identify what has been presented to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, that's useful guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, I'm not insisting on a literal translation because of course Mr. Krajisnik has summarised in his way and then most important is that we, without having full knowledge and full access to the text, that we at least know what is on the CD.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As I just said, that's useful guidance, Your Honour, and Mr. Jonovic is already carrying out that task and will do so in conjunction with his other court duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration, although it's a long time ago, but by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony. And Mr. Tieger are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Shortly before we adjourned yesterday, we had begun to address some of the specific strategic objectives and we were focused, immediately before the recess, the adjournment, on strategic objective number 3, as articulated by Dr. Karadzic at the 16th session of the RS Assembly, "The third strategic goal is to establish a corridor in the Drina valley, that is the elimination of the Drina as a border between two worlds. We are on both sides of the Drina and our strategic interest and our living space are up there." Now, we, Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Tieger, but I'm also looking at you, Mr. Krajisnik, often reference is made to the strategic objectives. Could we do it in a summary way to say the Neretva River or the Una river objective, and then I take it we all know what we are talking about, or access to the sea so we don't have to explain who said what and what the exact wording is. We are always referring to the heading as it was published in the Official Gazette. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We briefly compared the Drina River objective to the map with the red line, which you explained during the course of your examination-in-chief, and discussed briefly Dr. Karadzic's words. Now, the map that you produced during the course of your examination-in-chief, which we looked at yesterday and which is found at tab 228, is not the only map that we had an opportunity to see and -- or that you had an opportunity to see and discuss during the course of your examination-in-chief. We also saw you in front of an ethnic map of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the course of an interview that was on -- produced on television, and you were explaining at that time the territories possessed by the Bosnian Serbs. Now, we can take another look at that video, if necessary, Mr. Krajisnik, and we probably will during the course of the remaining examination, but as I recall, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Chamber would like to see it again, if you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excellent, Your Honour. It's at 213.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not at this very moment, if you're not prepared for it then, perhaps, but the Chamber would like to see it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's worth a minute or two to set it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Court is ready?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We are standing in front of the ethnic map of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- the former Bosnia and Herzegovina, with marked borders of the territory that is presently held by the Bosnian Serb army. I can only say that what was being said, the propaganda that we are holding territories ethnically populated by the other national communities, that is not true, which can be seen on the ethnic map of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which we can cover with a transparent sheet on which the territories are exactly marked, the territories held by our army, that those are in fact areas that belong to our people. A map, a similar one to this, as far as I'm informed, was offered in Geneva, and it was made clear that the Serbs want the borders of our future republic to be ... that is the Neretva River valley, and this is mostly territory of Republika Srpska. With the proviso that we allow for the possibility of certain enclaves on our territory that may be populated with the -- with other ethnic communities. Sarajevo is a separate problem. At the moment, it is marked as ... the area of city proper is marked as Muslim territory, but, in our relations, we will work for a demilitarisation and division between the two ethnic communities, primarily Serb and Muslim, and maybe a municipality for ... I mean a municipality populated by the Croatian community. The territory of Republika Srpska represents, in fact, the border along the Una River, the Sava River, with a smaller area that is not yet held by our forces, I mean, it's not liberated yet. That is Orasje, those are ... that is the border, this is the territory of Semberija, the territory of the Ozren mountain and the territory of Eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina. We presented, as our territory and our strategic goal to the Croatian community in Graz, that our border should be between our two ethnic communities, that would be the Neretva River. In any case, this continuity of our territory, it is ... it is in one piece, if I may say so, and we will do our best that there is one constituent unit of Republika Srpska, and allow the possibility of more constituent units for Croatian and Muslim people. Simply, that is not a condition. What is a condition is that our republic be an integral one and not divided into several parts."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm looking again at D192A, the map with the red squiggly line that you provided, and indicated represented the -- represented strategic objective number 3, the Drina River objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's tab 228, for Mr. Krajisnik's benefit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The territories taken by Bosnian Serb forces and pointed out by you in Eastern Bosnia in the video we have just seen bear a much closer relationship to Dr. Karadzic's articulation of strategic objective number 3 at the 16th session than does the red squiggly line depicted in D192A. In fact, Mr. Krajisnik, it is the -- it is correct to say that what Dr. Karadzic expressed at the 16th Assembly, that the strategic goal was that the Drina no longer be -- or the Drina would not be a border between two Serbian worlds or two Serbian states, was the strategic objective and not the red squiggly line in D192A; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not right. And I explained why it isn't right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, part of your explanation, Mr. Krajisnik, was that although Dr. Karadzic expressed himself in the way we have looked at repeatedly, he didn't really agree with himself about that. So I'd like to look to other expressions by Dr. Karadzic and others of strategic objective number 3. So could we first turn to tab 210, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if the Chamber wants to consider this map used during this television programme, it would have always to play that portion. Is there a possibility - I mean, nothing changes in the map - for very practical purposes to have a still to be made from that portion of the video so that you can look at it without using your technical equipment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Unless someone tells me to the contrary, Your Honour, I'm confident that can be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Josse --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Couldn't possibly object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it it doesn't have to be a separate exhibit. I mean, it's just a still taken from the video, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. No problem at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber would highly appreciate if you would produce that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll see to it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, tab 210 contains excerpts from the 34th Assembly session that is the 34th Republika Srpska Assembly session held on the 27th and 29th of August, 1993, and the 9th and 10th of September, 1993, and the 29th September and 1st of October of the same year. It's P65, Your Honour, but I need, clearly, more specific information for the Court on that, but -- and we will provide that. In the early part of the session, Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Karadzic is reminding the deputies and other persons assembled about the strategic goals, and if you would turn to the -- the Court would turn to page 14 of the English at the bottom, and Mr. Krajisnik, you would turn to page 12 of the B/C/S, that is 02150520, where Dr. Karadzic begins: "Strategic goals adopted by this Assembly have been or will be achieved to the fullest extent, just to remind those who do not know it. This Assembly reached strategic goals of Serb people which have become in a certain way our tasks, our obligation to realise them, but those were the goals we aimed at and the goals we aim at now to achieve whenever it would be possible." He then goes on to discuss the individual goals, and on page 15 of the English, and I believe still on the same page you began on in B/C/S, he again articulates the third goal by saying, "The third goal is to let the river of Drina be never more a border between Serb people." Mr. Krajisnik, it appears, therefore, that when Dr. Karadzic expressed the strategic goal relating to the Drina on May 12th, 1992, at the 16th session, he expressed exactly what he meant and exactly what the objective was, as he explained again at the 34th session. It wasn't a mistake, it wasn't something he disagreed with, it was in fact the goal. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly what I've been saying. A border is not only a physical border but also a psychological border, where there are no passports and such. When there is a border, you have to produce a passport. Well, you have that in several documents I've provided. This is Bosnia. This is about Bosnia. Bosnia cannot be without borders. In 1993, Bosnia and Herzegovina has its internationally recognised borders, and you can't say there won't be a border between Serbia and Bosnia. There will be no psychological border, though. There will be no passports. There is constant repeated reference to negotiations. Look here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we have addressed that before and retreating into the language of negotiations doesn't address the issue that we've been discussing, and that is that the strategic objectives articulated at the 16th session were intended to be pursued both militarily and through negotiations to finalise them. So citing language of negotiations doesn't suggest that there was in any way an elimination of or failure to pursue the military option of achieving results on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, that's not correct. You have a document that I produced today concerning the session of the Presidency of the 9th of June, 1992, with military men and politicians in attendance, and the last but one item on the agenda was to publish the strategic objectives and a map of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to send them to the European Community. Even then it was understood that it's a political objective. Only political. The military men were present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the one doesn't exclude the other, does it? I mean, if military men are there and do not disagree with sending certain plans to the negotiating table, does that mean in your view, is that correct, that then it's not -- in military terms they are silent, they say, okay, put it to the negotiations, and then it's off the table for military purposes, without any explicit word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the 9th of June is just a month after the strategic objectives were endorsed, and on the agenda of that meeting had the task to publish strategic objectives and send them to the European Community. Why would they be sending military objectives? I'm telling you what was said and what was understood on the 9th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, okay, I do understand if you say we send something to the negotiation table, then it's out of the mind of any soldier, of any military man, that as a support or if the negotiations fail, that it's not -- it's not within the realm of the military any more. If that's your testimony, then it's clear. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were other strategic objectives psychological in nature? That is, when Dr. Karadzic referred to the second goal or fourth goal, did he intend that to mean that the Bosnian Serbs would only -- that those were intended to be implemented psychologically rather than physically, that they weren't related to territories? Or was the third goal the only psychological goal?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Please, this second objective, the president said the objective was a corridor. With regard to the corridor I also provided material here. It was a government session of the 19th of June, where it was said that the issue of the corridor should be resolved, it has nothing to do with the strategic objective you have in this material of today. On the 12th of May, it was specified exactly: Through exchange of territories with Croats, we plan to resolve this politically. Look at the transcript of that session, and you'll see. And the fourth objective is what - Sarajevo. Find the 17th of March, or rather, the 19th of March in 1992. Karadzic said exactly what kind of objective Sarajevo was. I also produced some material, namely the ethnic -- Serb ethnic parts of Sarajevo. It's all documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will deal with Sarajevo and we will deal with the documentation shortly, but --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you said it was the fourth goal, didn't you? You mentioned Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's the fifth goal. In any event, we will be talking about that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I confused the objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine. I asked you that in particular because of course Dr. Karadzic says, at the 34th session which we are looking at now, and said at the 16th session, the second goal was to have connected territories. And about the fourth goal, he said the fourth goal is that the valley of the river of Neretva belong to East Herzegovina and/or Republika Srpska due to the historical and ethnic right, geographical and economic right. Those would appear to relate to the possession, the physical possession, of those territories rather than to any relationship psychological or otherwise to them. There is no dispute about that, is there, that at least the second and fourth goals related to territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both of them relate to territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then let's turn to tab 232, please. It's Dr. Karadzic again talking about the strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this will need a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1237, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, P1237 is a recording of Dr. Karadzic on the 23rd of August, 1995, by Banja Luka Television. And again, Dr. Karadzic is discussing the strategic goals, and he states: "It is our vital interest that the Una and the Sava become our borders --" I'm sorry, Your Honours, that's precisely in the middle of the page where it indicates "Begin Karadzic recording." That's the second paragraph in the first page. "It is our vital interest that the Una and the Sava become our borders, that the Drina be ours, for it is ours. It has been ours for centuries." And he continues that we get -- "that we get a part of Sarajevo for all of Sarajevo used to belong to the Serbs. To get a part of the Neretva valley and to gain access to the sea. These are the strategic goals that our Assembly adopted already in 1992. They were revealed later on. It was no longer a secret. These are our goals and our nation is fighting to realise them, to realise such a state and it has realised such a state. The international community must recognise that. Of course, not all of them are realised as long as there is fighting, until an international treaty is signed. Not an agreement between the warring sides but an international treaty which is the highest level, the highest legal and political intergovernmental act guaranteed by the world powers." Now, when Dr. Karadzic says, "The Drina is ours, and it has been ours for centuries --"

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon but what date is this? When was this statement made? Do you have the date perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: August 23rd, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I do apologise for having interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's not a problem, Mr. Krajisnik. When Dr. Karadzic says, "The Drina is ours, it has been ours for centuries," and he says it's one of the six strategic goals adopted by the Assembly in 1992, he's referring to the territory along the Drina, he's referring to that Eastern Bosnia territory, he's not referring to the fact that the Drina will belong to the Muslims but that the Serbs will be seeking some kind of visas or passports to enable them to pass through to Serbia. That's the truth of it, isn't it, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the truth, what you said, but it's not an answer to your question, and I can explain it. That's why I asked you what year we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Please explain.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the contact plan, the time we are talking about a plan, and it's a big problem, what territory we are going to take, whether in the east or in the west of Republika Srpska, because we have to have 49 per cent, and Mr. Karadzic is speaking about the importance of the Drina, that we should have certain territories along the Drina River. Now, everything that Mr. Karadzic says here he's saying so that the international community -- he's saying that the international community must verify our plans, not that we take control of the Drina. So this is related to the contact group's plan. I know that for certain, because the ethnic regions, our ethnic regions in the west, remained with the Muslims - Grahovo, Glamoc, Drvar, and so on - whereas we had in our possession in the eastern part along the Drina, important territories, so that's why Mr. Karadzic said that in figurative terms, the Drina is ours, having in mind the contact plan. Now, as far as this goal is concerned, it's exactly as I stated, why we had planned it that way, not to have Drina the border between these two worlds, and that is something that Mr. Izetbegovic confirmed, and he said this, that there shouldn't be any passports or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Izetbegovic did not stand in front of a map showing that the Bosnian Serb forces possessed the entirety of Eastern Bosnia and suggest in any way that that was consistent with anything he had said about borders and passports, and you know that. The strategic objective has nothing to do with that comment by Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I have explained here what I was explaining on the map, that the interruption, the break, in the statement, as I emphasised, is where a sentence was left out, that we are yielding to the Muslim side a narrow part of Sarajevo where there are more Serbs than in the whole of the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I said that and I remember that full well. So that was the break in this, what's it called, this recording, and I emphasised where that gap or break was, and I said, in the eastern part, where the majority of the population was Muslim, small, little areas, small towns. And I would have said quite the opposite if I were to say this is now Serb. And I think the map was a 1993 map or whenever. Perhaps it was 1992. Not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to tab 231, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would you mind if I ask one specific question in relation to what you pointed at at the map. Mr. Krajisnik, you said, "There was smaller area that's not yet held by our forces, I mean, it's not liberated yet. That is Orasje." Could you point exactly? Perhaps I could provide with you D192A.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Orasje is Croatian, there is no problem there. And that wasn't the correct statement on my part. Orasje was Croatian, along the Sava River. And you're quite right, we didn't have the right to Orasje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you said it still has to be liberated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I wasn't right there. I wasn't right on that score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please point at the map exactly where that is so that I've got a better idea.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Orasje is this bit here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it's inhabited by an absolute Croatian majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that. That's clear. And just for the record, you pointed at the first area at the northern border, which is at approximately one fourth coming from the east, which is not blue but of a different colour, small --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it says Croatian territory, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I want to look at a couple of comments made in the Assembly at different times concerning Podrinje or the Drina area. If you could look first at the comments of Mr. Dukic at the 25th session of the National Assembly held on 19 and 20 January, 1993, found at tab 231.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In particular the comment will be found in approximately the middle of the page, page 42, Your Honours, and at page 02149979 in the B/C/S, at the bottom of the first paragraph. And, Your Honour, I believe this will need a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1238, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Here, in January of 1993, Mr. Dukic, the former president of the SDS executive board, and someone whom you've mentioned during the course of your examination, Mr. Krajisnik, is complaining about the Vance-Owen Plan and what it offers the Serbs. And after highlighting certain aspects of the territory, including its economic implications, he states: "... according to the Vance map, Birac as a whole has been painted green. It is clear to everyone that there can be no Serbian state, nor a community of Serbian states, nor life or prospects for the Serbian people without Podrinje, from Foca to Bijeljina. Even Karadjordje knew that. Regrettably, we too have failed to settle the issue of this Podrinje over which world empires, ideologies and religions have clashed and are still clashing. Nowhere are the Serbs suffering more or are the prospects for their future poorer than in the Podrinje of today." Now, again, as was the case with the comment by Dr. Karadzic we looked at a few moments ago, Mr. Dukic refers to the Serbs' history in the Podrinje, and he says flatly that it's clear to everyone that the establishment of the Serbian state and its intended linkage with Serbia will require Bosnian Serb possession of that entire area, which is consistent with Dr. Karadzic's articulation of strategic objective number 3 at the 16th session and thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Karadzic didn't say that, and you're not right, unfortunately, Mr. Prosecutor, in what you say. This is quite a different set of problems, and I can explain what Dr. Dukic said here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So true -- correct or incorrect, that Mr. Dukic is saying that it's clear to everyone there could be no Serbian state without that entire swath of territory along Eastern Bosnia belonging to the Bosnian Serbs. You can explain why he said that, but he's saying that, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- what he said is, it is clear to everyone there is no Serb state, nor a community of Serb states, or life or any prospects for the Serb people without Podrinje from Foca to Bijeljina. That's what he said. He was looking at it from an economic standpoint because he was an economist himself, and he was discussing mines and the general wealth of the country and of course the territory as well, and on that point you're right, because he was referring to the historical genocide that was executed during World War II, but this is the economic principle that he was referring to and using here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So in addition to the historical genocide committed against the Serbs during World War II, Mr. Dukic was invoking an economic rationale for the necessity of Republika Srpska possessing that entire territory of Eastern Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the entire area, not the entire territory no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There would be some enclaves, as you've said repeatedly, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. When he's talking about economic indices, he's talking about the enclaves in which you have economic areas; mines, thermoelectric power stations, or rather, hydroelectric power stations, and so on and so forth. He's not talking about forests and fields, but when he says territory, he means in that territory, in that area or region. And you have that on the 6th of May, for instance, 1993. His entire presentation to the session, everything he said and everything he thought, that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Whatever the rationale, Mr. Krajisnik, invoked by various people, the significance of the Drina for Republika Srpska and the Serbian people was considered enormous, and the territories sought by Republika Srpska pursuant to strategic objective number 3 included those-- that entire area, some of which might be ceded to the Muslims in the form of small enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, that's not true. A quarter of the Drina River is the border. A quarter. I explained that last time. The rest is the border beyond the Drina. So the psychological border on the Drina is the problem. Passports, you can't go to Serbia, you can't have links with it. And I showed that. It's from Visegrad to Zvornik. That's all. All the rest is away from the Drina River border on which the Serbs have territory on both sides of the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn once again to the comments of -- first let me turn to Mr. -- Let me turn to the comments of Dr. Karadzic at the 33rd session, please. That's in July of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll move forward. We'll determine whether it needs a number or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, perhaps you would try to find out. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like to turn your attention to Dr. Karadzic's remarks at 02150376, the bottom half of that page in your version and, Your Honours, at page 53, where Dr. Karadzic begins.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May we have a tab reference, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's an extra that should have been provided to the booth. I don't know if -- you do have it, and it's an extra. It says on its cover, "Minutes and tape recording of the 33rd session of the RS National Assembly."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not on our cover but -- we have no cover page with it, but its last four digits English is 0497. B/C/S last four digits 0376.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it does need a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It doesn't?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1239, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that this was July, 1993, the Assembly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 33rd session, held on the 20th and 21st of July, 1993. At the beginning of his remarks, Dr. Karadzic is talking about the UN as an important factor, indicating that we have to crawl slowly and wisely between Scylla and Charybdis, trying not to cause resistance because it does not matter to us. But then he continues on to the next page in English, same page in B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik, stating: "They have not recognised borders of Republika Srpska yet. Gorazde is ours. We might make some concessions in the area of Sarajevo itself so that Gorazde could remain ours. The significance of the Drina for Republika Srpska and Serbian people is enormous. Finally, one of the strategic objectives is that the Drina is not a border. We decided about it here at this Assembly." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, Gorazde was a predominantly Muslim municipality, correct? One of the many predominantly Muslim --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was a predominantly Muslim municipality, Gorazde was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Dr. Karadzic is saying there that in view of the significance of that area for Republika Srpska and the Serbian people, in view of the fact that one of the strategic objectives is that the Drina is not a border, that Gorazde, then held by or effectively controlled by, the Bosnian Serbs, should remain "ours." That's a reflection of the fact that the -- that strategic objective number 3 --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. The subject was to send Gorazde -- to send UN observers to Gorazde, and the deputies were against this, and that is why Karadzic says how important the Drina is to us. And we wanted to send UN observers. That's what we were aiming for. So that was the reason he's referring to Gorazde. Not the strategic goal. He said that it was important to us, that the Drina was important to us, but just a little way before that, you'll find that explanation, because it was a protected area and the UN observers were supposed to be in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What -- well, let's turn to tab 235.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This needs a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1240, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, I do understand that the observers, at least, the UN was a -- was an element of this discussion. Gorazde at that time was militarily controlled by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Muslims. And to the end of the war it was controlled by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this period of time in July, 1993, it was still held by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. The Muslims, and it was a protected area, and the UN observers were supposed to be in Gorazde, and the deputies were opposed to that, so that's why Karadzic was saying this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, he wants Gorazde to, as he said, it is yours, and he says that by making some other concessions, that Gorazde could remain yours. That seems not to be just related to sending military observers but it seems to relate to what the final outcome would be, that is that an area, as you said, controlled by the Muslims at that time, would finally become Serb, although it is a Muslim-majority area or territory. I mean, that's not limited to sending observers, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. It says we'll have to give concessions in Sarajevo. I know that there was a discussion going on whereby parts of Serb Sarajevo should be exchanged for Gorazde. That was a discussion in the negotiations, but that was never realised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in the first lines he expresses after he has said that one should try to keep Gorazde as yours, he immediately follows then by saying how important the Drina is and that it is one of the strategic objectives that the Drina is not a border. So he seems to pronounce that in almost one breath, the efforts to keep Gorazde and the significance of the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, the subject of discussion is the sending of observers, and now he's saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying -- yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to protect -- or rather, the protected area to be protected from the observers, that is to say who is attacking whom, Mr. Karadzic says that we are interested in Gorazde too but we'll have to make that concession, and it says part of Sarajevo, but all this is linked to sending the observers. It has nothing to do with strategic goals or objectives. He takes this as a justification in order to send the observers there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic is mentioning strategic objectives and if you say it has got nothing to do with that, that's not easy to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. No. He does mention that the Drina is a strategic goal to justify why the observers are going to Gorazde so that he could put that through the Assembly, and he says you can't have the Assembly as being an executive organ. You can't decide whether the observers will go or not, he says to the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, he says it immediately following a line which says that, through making concessions, Gorazde could remain Serb, not textually. The link is there not for sending observers, but textually the link is there between -- to Gorazde to remain or by concessions. Clearly refers to negotiations and making concessions. But then Gorazde to remain Serbian and not Gorazde to be observed by UN military. But I'm just trying to fully understand how you interpret these words of Mr. Karadzic. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you have here further up in the text, Mr. President, you have a passage about the observers. On that same page, it refers to observers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't miss that the discussion starts with observers but what I'm trying to find out is it seems that although it's still about -- it starts with observers, but the passage certainly does not end focusing on observers but ends on a subject which may be related, but certainly is not focusing on sending of observers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but how to keep Gorazde as a result of concessions to be made in respect of Sarajevo, and a reference close to that line, to the objective -- strategic objectives. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. You are absolutely right. That's what it is precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We saw this morning, or saw documentation this morning, of Dr. Karadzic referring to the Drina as "ours." Dr. Karadzic's concern at the 33rd with respect to Gorazde is at least in part the concern that Gorazde might connect with another enclave of the Muslims or in some manner prevent the Drina from being "ours" and prevent the objective of the Drina not being a border between Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain what the issue was, if that's your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, my -- Dr. Karadzic is concerned about Gorazde and its enormous significance, that is the enormous significance of the Drina, because he doesn't want Gorazde in any way to prevent the Drina from being Serb, or Bosnian Serb, and he doesn't want Gorazde to undercut the goal of the third strategic objective, to ensure that that area is not a border between Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not true. He wouldn't be sending UN observers, he wouldn't be wanting to send UN observers, if that were true. He is, on the contrary, justifying the sending of observers, the idea of sending observers, with that story.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look, then, at your remarks at the 34th session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I again ask you, Mr. Krajisnik, the lines prior to that say, "If we can carry ten kilograms today instead of 100, which they would load on us tomorrow, then we should rather take ten kilograms ourselves and proceed, because if we wait, they will load us with 100 kilograms tomorrow." Which seems to be an expression, but please correct me if I'm wrong, that one should develop a strategy in which you take today what you can take or you can bear and then what the future will bring us, then, is still to be expected. So therefore if you say why would he have sent observers to Gorazde at this time? One would be inclined to interpret this in the context of what is today -- could develop in whatever way tomorrow, and therefore not to give a too significant meaning to the step taken at that very moment. One might be inclined to interpret it that way, but if you'd like to comment on that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm going to say now is the real interpretation. Karadzic said it's better for us to accept observers, 20 of them, than a whole UN army, because the assemblymen were afraid that the latter would be arming the Muslims who would be attacking Serbs, and that they would get weapons by airlift. He said, it's better to accept observers than a whole battalion of troops. Because the UN plays an important role. That's what he said. And UNPAs were in fact armed. That is true. Although that was late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in connection with Dr. Karadzic's remarks about the Drina being "ours," and the concern that Muslim-held territories would be in conflict with the goal of the third strategic objective, to prevent the Drina from being a border, I asked you to turn to tab 210, which reflects remarks at the 34th Assembly session. I had indicated to the Court earlier that was P65, and I had a better number for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, the 34th session at tab 210, Mr. Krajisnik. And if the Court could turn to page 129, and Mr. Krajisnik, you could turn to 02150643. And, Your Honours this is P64A tab 37, P65, tab 221. And there, Mr. Krajisnik, you state: "Third strategic goal was Drina. I think that we should task our negotiating team not to allow Muslim side request that Zepa gets connected with Gorazde an enclave to be accepted, because in that case, Drina would not be ours. They would have their own republic and we would enable it in that way. And we would fulfil at least 80 to 90 per cent of this plan that Drina is not actually a border between Serbs." Now, again, Mr. Krajisnik, you're talking about -- you're talking to the Assembly members in the context of negotiations, again you're talking about the possibility of accepting more than your ultimate objectives, but you are also there reminding the deputies of what those objectives are, in particular the third objective, which encompassed ensuring that the Drina was "ours" and that it would not actually be a border between Serbs. The same thing that Dr. Karadzic was talking about; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. You see here what exactly I said. When we were adopting it, it was the second corridor, and this is later, I don't know when, in 1993, when we had a plan on our agenda. It was already the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. And the problem was Brcko. Right it was the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan that gave us three enclaves in the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Correct. This is the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan that came after the Vance Plan, and I'm saying that the second --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is unclear what Mr. Krajisnik said, the interpreters apologise. It was the second something was the corridor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the interpreters could not hear the last part of your sentence. You said, "... and I'm saying that the second --" and then they couldn't follow you any more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, on page that ends with 634, Momcilo Krajisnik says, "Another strategic goal was a corridor. We called it corridor then because the objectives that we have now attained were still remote, whereas this plan discussed here was October, 1993, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, and I can give you a map to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reference to second strategic goal is found on page 128, at approximately the 10th line down from where Mr. Krajisnik begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in the context of talking about the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan to the deputies, you remind them of the third strategic goal and, once again, articulate what it's about in order to assist them in assessing the advantages and disadvantages of that plan. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third or the second? You've been reading to me from the second.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I read to you originally the --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. Yes. Correct. This is the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, wherein they linked up with the road cutting our territory in two, and I said that shouldn't be done but that instead enclaves should remain. All of it is about the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's look quickly at remarks by Mr. Mijatovic at the 53rd Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And may I produce tomorrow the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan that would explain this? Precisely from that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- I leave it to the parties whether there is any -- let's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, it's opened it up, in my submission. That's the answer of the witness, and it's opened it up to go into that in some detail now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: His answer is very clear to the robust suggestion my learned friend put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, I'll reread who exactly opened it up, whether it was opened up by the question or by the answer. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tab 235, Mr. Krajisnik. These are the remarks of Mr. Mijatovic at the 53rd session of the RS National Assembly on 28 August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It needs a number, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We assigned it --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at page 51 of the B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik, at the -- that is 02154350, approximately 12 lines from the bottom, and at page 41 of the English, Your Honours, just below the middle of the page, the -- for reference purposes, the Court looks down at the right-hand column, about -- a short portion below the middle, you'll see a reference to "a clean Drina." I'm going to read from that sentence. Mr. Mijatovic states,

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "There are --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find it. You said 53rd session. I'm in tab 235; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you referred to the B/C/S page 51. My start with 87 and then 88. I do not see any 51 there. I can find 41, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 41 in the English, Your Honour, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see. It's split up into -- yes, that always confuses me a bit. If you start with the English and then have some B/C/S, then comes some English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have the same problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will see a short, first full paragraph that says, "For those reasons ..." the next paragraph beginning, "The fact is that they have ..." and then if the Court goes down 15 lines, there is very left -- there is, for purposes of identification, you'll see RS down that -- at the -- one of the far left, and then the sentence after that states: "There are two or three goals of RS that this Assembly defined at its first session in Banja Luka, that is access to the sea, the Neretva River valley, a clean Drina, participation of the Herzegovina Corps in the possible division of Sarajevo, et cetera." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Mijatovic's reference to "a clean Drina" is again a reference to strategic objective number 3, and its goal of ensuring that Eastern Bosnia would be in the possession of the Bosnian Serbs in order to ensure that that territory remained "ours" and that it was not a border between two Serb states or two Serb worlds. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This was not a goal. You know that. It's how he interprets it in 1995 when a specific plan was topical, in order to get as many territories in the eastern part of Republika Srpska as possible. This is the plan of the contact group. He's actually calling on those strategic goals in order to get the map to be as good as possible. Mistakenly, of course. There are many other mistakes he made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He is calling on the strategic goals, and he's explaining what they mean, and he's saying, essentially, what I put to you at the beginning of my questions about strategic objective number 3, that it meant that the Drina area was not to be a border between two Serb worlds but the backbone of two Serb worlds. Isn't that right? Isn't that what strategic objective number 3 was about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not the objective. I told you, one-fourth of the Drina forms a border between Bosnia and Serbia. So the rest of the border is not the Drina. Other features formed the border. In Bosnia and Herzegovina the border is only two-thirds of the river. Only from Zvornik to Bijeljina. Look at the map and you'll see. And that was held by the Serbs. That's what Serbs used as crossing, not other parts. But what is meant is the psychological border. Serbs were on both sides of the river in Bijeljina so you could cross over without a passport. That's what he meant. And he's making here an interpretation of the contact group plan and trying to achieve as good positions as possible. He himself is from Bijeljina, from Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before the break let's turn to your own remarks on November 1st, 1995, in -- article in Srpska Oslobodjenje. I think that's an extra, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would receive number? Would that be P1241, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's an Oslobodjenje article, 1st of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, P1241, in front of you now, Mr. Krajisnik, should be at least somewhat familiar to you. It's an article in Srpska Oslobodjenje from November, 1995. And if you'll look to page 5, it has two pictures of you there, and at the bottom of the left -- the second to the left column, and beginning at the very top of the right-hand column, you'll see the remarks to which I'm going to direct your attention. So it would be immediately opposite the bottom picture of you. And it begins, "I will remind you of something." You see that, Mr. Krajisnik? And in the English, Your Honours -- the English. You got the translation before you. "I will remind you of something. At the beginning of the war, we adopted six strategic goals. The first was to separate ourselves from Muslims --"

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not getting translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said -- I'm sorry, I can't find it. Because it's my interview, I really want to find this passage. You said it was opposite or above the photo?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, if you look in my direction, you see that page, the large page with the two photos?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the end, and you said above.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you'll look to that portion opposite the picture at the bottom, in that small -- in the left-hand column, beneath the header. "I will remind you of something. At the beginning of the war we adopted six strategic goals."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And continuing: "The first was to separate ourselves from Muslims and Croats. We did not say that we would create a state, even though we will have started with the creation of a state at a later stage. Then we asked for a corridor to link the western and eastern part, and we will continue to insist on this. The third thing was that the Drina must not be the border but the backbone of the Serbian people except for Gorazde." And then you continued discussing the fourth, fifth, and six goals, and conclude, "All the strategic objectives that our soldiers and our people died for, all these strategic goals are within our reach." That's a reflection in your own words, Mr. Krajisnik, of the fact that the third strategic objective was intended to ensure that the Drina would not be a border, as you said, but the backbone, between those two Serbian worlds, just as Dr. Karadzic said on May 12th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I did repeat the term "backbone." I did. But I assure you, it says here precisely "except Gorazde." A moment ago you were trying to persuade me that we wanted to take Gorazde. Here it says the contrary. This is about Dayton. There was a map, and that map is still in existence. We had already agreed the aims with Mr. Holbrooke that Republika Srpska would be in one piece, and I'm talking about the objectives that we have to attain at Dayton. This is before Dayton. And, of course, I was putting it roughly, without specifying. But I'm assuring you that it's not what you think it is. I was referring to a border that we could just go through. Why would I otherwise say backbone if there is no border between Bosnia and Serbia. Look at the beginning, we had already given up on a state. I read it here in the beginning. We made a sacrifice and abandoned the idea of Yugoslavia, a state. You cannot have a backbone if there are two states. I'll read you -- I'll read to you another quotation from this same article.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I think the imagery of backbone is pretty clear, Mr. Krajisnik, especially in this context. A backbone is that portion that supports and is between what roughly amounts to a single entity, and that's what you meant there.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. Please, if it's highlighted here, we made a great sacrifice. We abandoned the idea of our own state and accepted a Bosnian union in order to get an entrance ticket for a common delegation. That's what I said in that article. Here it is, at the top of the article. Even cultural linkage, educational linkage with Serbia would be special ties. We even accepted Bosnia as a state. If I read this whole article, I guarantee that I didn't say any different from what I testified here. I know exactly what my approach was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could we perhaps move to your next question. This is what Mr. Krajisnik has explained to us --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- quite a couple of times, that what the Drina not being a border meant to him, and just to further analyse newspapers, articles of which we do not even know whether these are exactly the words of Mr. Krajisnik, and apart from the explanations given already, it doesn't assist the Chamber very much. Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Mr. Krajisnik referred to other parts of this article --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He wants to draw our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was going to inquire whether the Prosecution intended to have the rest of it translated. I was concerned about context, and I emphasise that was before the witness said what he has just said. Having said that, if the Chamber is saying this article doesn't really assist them in their deliberations, then I'm certainly not going to pursue the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I still would have to discuss with my colleagues whether it would have the minimal weight as I at this moment might have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, if the Chamber are prepared to give that indication, it would certainly help the Defence. I don't know what my learned friend's position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I seem not to be the only one in this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not asking it to be translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I leave to the Court, of course, its assessment of weight. I want to point out, however, that this is an official -- Srpska Oslobodjenje had the official imprimatur of RS, was praised by Mr. Krajisnik himself, so to that extent, it's not just another newspaper article. Now the content is another story, and I leave that to the Court, but I don't want the Court to be misled about the nature of the publication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It doesn't change our mind, as far as requesting a translation of the whole of the newspaper article and, of course, Mr. Josse, it's up to you if there are other portions which you would like to draw our attention to, of course, you're fully free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. No. Let's not proceed. Let's have a break. We will adjourn until five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, earlier this morning, we talked about borders between Bosnia and Serbia. I think that was about 9.30 of your testimony. Republika Srpska, and Serbia and so on. When we looked at the video showing you at the ethnic map, indicating the territories held by the Bosnian Serbs, it clearly appeared that there would be no border of any non-Serb entity between Republika Srpska and Serbia at that time, or at least, based on the territories that you were indicating. What was the border in Eastern Bosnia as of late 1992, according to Republika Srpska authorities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That map is a proposal put forth to the international community. We wanted the enclaves that were Muslim in the eastern part to be exchanged for certain Serb territories. So that's a proposal. That was the proposal that was sent to the European Community, or rather, to the negotiators. In fact, in 1992, there was Srebrenica, Gorazde - I don't know what else - Zepa, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the Assembly declared what the border of Republika Srpska was in Eastern Bosnia and other portions of what was determined to be or sought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask one thing? Mr. Krajisnik, you say that the map, so that's a proposal, that was the proposal that we sent to the European Community. In your comment, you start saying, "We are standing in front of the ethnic map of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. We've marked borders of the territory that is presently held by the Bosnian Serb army." I'm trying to reconcile the map as being a proposal and a map characterised in this television clip as presenting the territory presently held by the Bosnian Serb army. Could you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two maps. One is on the foil and the other one is underneath. And we sent a similar map to the European Community. I think that that is contained in that interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But where we find the borders, from what I remember, the underlying map is the ethnic map. And the borders, when you speak these words, you see the borders. And I mean, an ethnic map of course - at least that's my understanding - could not reflect territory held by, because then every ethnic bit or piece --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I took it that the map with the line on it was the map reflecting the territory presently held by the Bosnian Serb army. That's how I understood that comment. Now, if you say a proposal, a proposal similarly, I would say, could not be just reflecting the ethnic composition, because then you would have this very complicated picture. So even your answer has not reconciled where you now said that the map was a proposal - that's the map with the lines, because proposals are about lines and not about ethnic composition, I would think - whereas in the television clip you said it's the territory presently held. Unless, of course, the proposals would completely be in accordance with the territory you held at that time, but that was not my understanding until now. Could you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor asked me about 1992, and I said that in 1992, Srebrenica was in Muslim hands. Zepa, Gorazde as well. All of that is on the Drina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. Yes. The question said, if we are looking at the video showing you at the ethnic map, that it clearly appeared that there would be no border, et cetera, et cetera. The question then was what was the border in Eastern Bosnia as of late 1992 according to the Republika Srpska authorities? And then you said, that map is a proposal. You were not asked about whether the map was a proposal or reflected reality, but I nevertheless would like to know, is this map now giving a proposal or is the map reflecting the territory actually held by the Republika Srpska armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether this is contained in the stenographic notes, but my understanding was that I was asked where the Muslim border was on the border. I understood this to mean where are the areas that are border areas on the Drina. Now I'll explain the map, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'd like to have an answer to my question but I do agree with you that the question was not clear because whether in the eastern -- in Eastern Bosnia, when we are talking about borders, it could be borders between Serbian held territory within Bosnia and Herzegovina and the border with Muslim-held territory, where it could also refer to borders between Serbian-held parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia proper. So therefore the question, I would agree with you, was not entirely clear, at least it was not to me, but I nevertheless would like to have an answer to my question whether the map you're standing in front of with the flip-over on it, the lines on it, does that reflect a proposal or does it reflect the Serbian held territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From this point of view, I cannot say what map it was, because in 1992, if it was in 1992, I could not say that we were holding Srebrenica, Gorazde and Zepa when we were not holding that. Well, we couldn't have. We certainly couldn't have. Up until the end of the war, that was in Muslim hands. That's why I'm perplexed too when it says that it's held by our armed forces because we did not hold that, and that's a well known fact. But at the same time, I said this is the map that we gave to the international community, so that is how I tried to explain this to myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And any other respect, I do understand, and you gave some comment on enclaves, especially in the Drina area. You did not comment on any other matters, such as, well, for example, Prijedor being under Muslim control --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Okay. That's -- let's move on. And perhaps about the borders, Mr. Tieger, could you clearly --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll make it as clear as possible, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, didn't the Bosnian Serb Assembly declare that the indisputable border of Republika Srpska was the -- in the east, that is the eastern border, was the border with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and didn't that happen in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right. The border is on the Drina, from Bijeljina to Zvornik, yes, that's Serb territory. If that's it, then yes, that's it. You know what? Along the border with Yugoslavia, on the Drina, there are few Muslim territories. Well, maybe this is not very clear. Perhaps I should try to explain it a bit better. I'm trying to guess what you're looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm simply asking you about an issue that was raised before, and that is where Republika Srpska determined the boundaries of its territory to be, and so my question is, and I think you answered it but you can clarify if not, that at the 17th Assembly session --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I did not answer, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, let me tell you something. The 17th session was two months after the 12th of May. We never determined the borders of Republika Srpska. We always said that they would be agreed upon at the peace negotiations. If there were some discussions and explanations, they weren't conclusions. So that's a different matter. And those were objections made to us, that we didn't have any borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we can clarify this by turning to the transcript of the 17th session itself, at page 103 and 104 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please get one for me, too?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik, once -- you don't have that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me just get it. I'm so sorry. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you would turn, Mr. Krajisnik, to page 02149599, those are the concluding remarks that you made at that session, beginning at the bottom of 9599, and Your Honours, at the bottom of page 103. You stated: "Before we close, since we have finished with the agenda, last night we discussed the borders. I move that the Assembly adopt the text because we discussed it last night, only the borders. And that we adopt the text today for the sake of the minutes. Aiming to end the hostilities and protect the civilians as well as to enable the functioning of the rule of law, the Assembly of Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina at its 17th session held on 25 July, 1992, brought unanimously a decision on establishing disputable and indisputable borders of its territory in the following ways: The indisputable borders are, the western border is the Una River, the northern border is the Sava River, the eastern border is the border with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the southern border is just one part of the border with Croatia, the south-west border is partly the border with Croatia and partly with the Republic of Serb Krajina." And then you go on to identify the disputable borders, indicate at the bottom that those borders shall be subject to corrections and verifications in accordance with international agreements and indicate below that the Assembly has adopted the statement unanimously. So it is correct, Mr. Krajisnik, that the declared border of Republika Srpska as of July, 1992, was the border with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. From Zvornik to Bijeljina. Certainly. That's where our border was with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. You see, from Visegrad onwards, there is Rudo, Cajnice, so on, all of that is our territory, but we are not talking about the entire border. Not all of the Drina River is the border between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina but only a small part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Republika Srpska was struggling to establish itself and control territory that would be recognised by the international community and to identify the borders of that entity but everybody knew where the borders of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were, and that --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that territory coincides with exactly what is depicted in the ethnic map where you are pointing out the territories controlled by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the month of July, and that map was much later. The map came later, because I have that black ribbon after August, 1992. On that map I'm wearing the black ribbon because my wife had died, so that's not it. This is where we established the disputed and undisputed territories, we did not establish the borders of Republika Srpska. We just established what was disputed and what was not disputed, because after this session we embarked on negotiations, and now what was it that we were supposed to advocate at these negotiations? From this session, we went to the London Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina what's the difference between the territory controlled by the Bosnian Serbs as indicated on that map and the border of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me about this Assembly or the map? If you're asking about the map, I'll explain the map. If you're asking me about the session, I'll explain the session but, please, do not link up the two. They are totally unrelated. I cannot explain this which came later. I already said that. But this is different. Over there, Neretva is the border, and here Neretva is not in dispute, so there are hundreds of things that are different. On the map, the Neretva is the border, whereas here, that territory is in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wasn't asking about the Neretva. I was asking about the area in Eastern Bosnia, Podrinje, the Drina, the area that we have been discussing in connection with strategic objective number 3. In July, the Assembly declared that that border would be the border with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. When we look at the map, it seems to encompass the territories held by the Bosnian Serb appear to encompass that entire territory along that border. Is that right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, please, as for this particular point, from the southernmost part of eastern Republika Srpska, all the way up to Gorazde, the border is not on the Drina. And that is Serb territory. And then you skip over to Zvornik, and then from Zvornik to Bijeljina the border is on the Drina and that is Serb territory and that's where the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is. Only between Visegrad and Zvornik is there Muslim territory. Gorazde is not the border with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It's only behind Gorazde. So that's where we have the border with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in certain sections.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, maybe I'm -- can I ask you to turn to tab 229 very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you can see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you a quick question. The green represents the territory of what -- what was Bosnia and Herzegovina, at least at the beginning of 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand. The green, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is Bosnia-Herzegovina, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes, yes, Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes, yes. We can put it on the map, or rather, we can put this map here, and then I can explain what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If it's necessary I'll be happy to do that. To the right is Serbia and Montenegro as we see labelled on the map.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the difference between the green and the white is the border of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And, please, can I just explain what I was trying to say? Can we just put the map here on the ELMO? I'll explain what we wanted. All of this is the border, up to here, objective 3, all of that is the border with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, if you want to point at something, it should be done on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, please, I would like to ask for that. This is the border with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, all the way up to here, this part here. And up here, this is Serb territory, from this part here -- no, sorry, from this part here. Now, this is the Drina. That belongs to the Muslim part. And we have a border with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; all of this. So it's not this part here but this part down here as well. Herzegovina, that's ours. I actually wrote that down here, over here. That's the part -- well, Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde is here, Mr. President, right here. It's not on the border. Rudo is behind it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, one additional question. You said, on from Zvornik, up to Bijeljina, that's Serb territory. Now you have explained to us in quite some detail that we should look at territories not just by majority in a municipality, but to look more detailed at certain parts which would, although in a majority A municipality --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would nevertheless be a majority B community or village or town. Now, if I look at the map you presented to us, that is D192A, which is the more detailed map with even the red marking you made on that, I see that there are at least some of the border areas, although in a Serb majority municipality, seem not to be really Serb territories in the sense that there may have been, at the border there, majorities -- other ethnic majorities. So you already explained to us and emphasised very much that we should not just look at the majority beyond municipality, but what you seem to do here, yourself, is to claim that it was all Serb territory, although we find here villages or at least areas, territories, which are not on your own map depicted as of Serb majority. So I'm just wondering what approach we then should take. Now you say this is Serb territory, and on your own map it's not depicted as such, unless you look at it municipality by municipality, not in further detail, but you emphasised that we had to look at it in further detail and not just municipality by municipality. Could you please clarify that on what basis you now say that especially the border area that's all Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please just have the map that you're talking about placed here? And then I can explain. I'll explain here in a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tab 228, the first -- the first map in 228. Tab 228 is missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somebody stole my map, Mr. President. That is really -- and I'm so enamoured of this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it is with us, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's with you, then that is a cause for special concern. Now, Mr. President, this is the border. All of this is the border with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Now, I was saying that we have a border here, Herzegovina and Montenegro, right here.
